To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the bottom of the pyrite conduction band consists mainly of a low intensity sulfur p band; (2) the sulfur p band is of the same intensity as the contribution from disorder; (3) the sulfur p states appear on the pyrite surface; (4) the presence of low energy surface states may explain the low open-circuit voltage observed in experiments.

(1) the low intensity conduction band onset in pyrite is caused by a sulfur p-band that appears at a lower energy than the high intensity onset, (2) the sulfur p-band has the same magnitude of absorption as the contributions from defects and structural disorder, (3) this low intensity conduction state appears on the surface and is therefore likely to contribute to surface recombination and (4) we suggest that misidentified conduction bands may be a common occurrence in materials.
the bottom of FeS2’s conduction band is not as simple as previously assumed, and that the bandgap is not as wide as commonly assumed.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the electronic properties of the pyrite conduction band and the implications for absorption, OCV and surface recombination in pyrite solar cells.
the identification of the low energy sulfur band and its implications for absorption, OCV and surface recombination.
understanding the electronic properties of pyrite that may explain its low open-circuit voltage.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a bandgap of 0.95 e V is not a realistic value for FeS2, and that the bandgap of this material is likely to be much smaller.
the OCV of FeS2 is lower than previously assumed because of an underestimated bandgap.
pyrite is a promising material for solar technologies, however, it is not yet clear whether the low OCV is caused by a bandgap problem, or by a surface recombination problem, or both.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the bandgap of pyrites should be lowered to ∼0.5 e V and that the low intensity conduction bands should be considered when designing solar devices.
the sulfur p-band should be included in the fundamental bandgap and the OCV of pyrite, and it may also be a general problem in other materials.
the band structure of pyrite is more complicated than previously assumed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the bandgap of a material is not necessarily equal to the onset of absorption, and that the latter may not necessarily be the same for different materials.
the bandgap of pyrites is likely to be much lower than the value of ∼0,95 eV commonly quoted in the literature.

the conduction band structure of pyrite is more complicated than commonly thought, and the low intensity sulfur p-state may be responsible for the discrepancy between the fundamental bandgap and the OCV, as well as the low OCV itself.
